summary: Specifies the Ad hoc On-Demand Distance Vector routing protocol for mobile nodes in ad hoc networks. It adapts quickly to changing links, uses little processing, memory, and network capacity, and finds unicast routes to destinations in the network on demand. It is an experimental specification.

eli5.summary: When phones or gadgets form a network with no fixed wires and keep moving, paths change. This memo defines a way to find a route only when you need it, instead of keeping maps of everything.

questions: ad hoc on demand distance vector
how do ad hoc networks find routes
subtitle: On-demand routing for mobile ad hoc networks: find a route only when you need one.

tldr.problem: Mobile nodes in an ad hoc network move around, so links break and topology changes. Keeping routes to every destination up to date would waste capacity.
tldr.mechanism: A node broadcasts a Route Request when it needs a route. The destination or a node with a fresh enough route unicasts a Route Reply back. Destination sequence numbers keep routes loop-free, and Route Errors report broken links.
tldr.outcome: AODV gives quick, loop-free route discovery with little control traffic and is designed for networks whose nodes trust each other. It is an Experimental RFC.

today: RFC 3561 is an Experimental RFC and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself says AODV defines no special security measures.

sections.title: Overview of AODV
sections.content:
The Ad hoc On-Demand Distance Vector (AODV) algorithm gives dynamic, self-starting, multihop routing between mobile nodes that form an ad hoc network. Nodes get routes quickly for new destinations and need not keep routes to destinations not in active communication. Operation is loop-free, and it avoids the Bellman-Ford counting to infinity problem.

A distinguishing feature is the destination sequence number, created by the destination and sent with any route information. Given two routes, a requesting node MUST pick the one with the greatest sequence number.

The RFC states AODV is designed for networks with tens to thousands of mobile nodes and for nodes that can all trust each other, through preconfigured keys or because no malicious intruders exist.
sections.eli5: AODV finds a way only when you need one. Each answer carries a freshness number, so you always pick the newest and never go around in circles.

sections.title: Finding and Maintaining Routes
sections.content:
AODV defines Route Request (RREQ), Route Reply (RREP) and Route Error (RERR) messages, sent over UDP to port 654. When a node needs a route it broadcasts a RREQ. The route is found when the RREQ reaches the destination or an intermediate node with a fresh enough route, meaning a valid entry whose sequence number is at least as great as the one in the RREQ.

Each node that handles the RREQ caches a reverse route to the originator, so the RREP can be unicast back. Nodes drop duplicate RREQs seen within PATH_DISCOVERY_TIME, identified by originator address and RREQ ID.

To limit flooding, the originator SHOULD use an expanding ring search: start with TTL_START, grow the TTL by TTL_INCREMENT after each timeout up to TTL_THRESHOLD, then use NET_DIAMETER. Repeated discovery MUST use binary exponential backoff, up to RREQ_RETRIES retries.

Nodes watch the next hop of active routes, using link-layer feedback, Hello messages or other means. On a break, a node invalidates routes, increments their sequence numbers and sends a RERR to the neighbors on its precursor lists. A node MAY try local repair if the destination is within MAX_REPAIR_TTL hops.
sections.eli5: You shout a question outward in bigger and bigger circles. The answer travels back the way the question came, and if a link breaks, everyone who relied on it gets told.

sections.title: The Four Message Types
sections.content:
Each message starts with a one-byte Type: RREQ is 1, RREP is 2, RERR is 3 and RREP-ACK is 4.

The RREQ has flags J, R, G, D and U, a Hop Count, an RREQ ID, the destination address and sequence number, and the originator address and sequence number. The G flag asks for a gratuitous RREP to the destination, D means only the destination may answer, and U means the destination sequence number is unknown.

The RREP carries a Prefix Size, Hop Count, destination address and sequence number, originator address and a Lifetime in milliseconds. Its A flag requires a RREP-ACK, used over links that may be unreliable or unidirectional. The RERR has an N (no delete) flag, a DestCount of at least 1 and the unreachable destinations with their sequence numbers.
sections.eli5: There are four kinds of notes: a question, an answer, a bad-news note and a 'got your answer' note.

sections.title: Defaults and Extensions
sections.content:
The RFC lists default parameters, and says performance is sensitive to them and they depend on the link layer. Hello messages are RREP messages with TTL 1, sent every HELLO_INTERVAL when the node has sent no other broadcast. A Hello Interval extension (type 1) lets a node advertise a different interval.

Subnet routers can answer for a whole prefix using the Prefix Size field, and the node with the lowest IP address is elected subnet router. A node that reboots waits DELETE_PERIOD before sending route discovery messages, because it may have lost its sequence numbers and neighbors might still use it as a next hop.
sections.eli5: The memo gives starting settings for timers and limits, like how often to say hello, that each network can tune.

sections.title: Security and Registries
sections.content:
AODV does not specify any special security measures, although routing protocols are prime targets for impersonation. If network membership is known and attacks are a danger, control messages must be protected with authentication such as cryptographic digests or signatures, and IPsec AH is called an appropriate choice. RREP messages SHOULD be authenticated to avoid spurious routes, and RERR messages SHOULD be authenticated to prevent route disruption.

IANA created registries for the message Type on port 654 (RREQ 1, RREP 2, RERR 3, RREP-ACK 4) and for the extension Type (Hello Interval 1). The RFC says IPv6 operation changes only that the address fields are enlarged.
sections.eli5: AODV trusts everyone by default, so a liar could send fake directions. In a network with a known membership, messages should be signed.
